hypotheses.mechanism: In AMMStandardHook._getOrFetchTokenSettings (line 907-919), when the hook has never been explicitly synced for a token (initialized=false in local cache), it lazy-fetches the HookTokenSettings struct from the registry via SETTINGS_REGISTRY.getTokenSettings(token) (line 912). This call returns the struct including non-zero whitelist IDs (pairedTokenWhitelistId, lpWhitelistId, poolTypeWhitelistId). However, the hook's local EnumerableSet caches for those IDs — _pairTokenWhitelists[id], _lpWhitelists[id], _poolTypeWhitelists[id] — are EMPTY because only the struct was transferred, not the whitelist contents. Immediately after the lazy-fetch, _validateTokenTradingRules (line 685-689) checks _pairTokenWhitelists[tokenSettings.pairedTokenWhitelistId].contains(pairedToken), which returns false for any pairedToken because the set is empty. All swaps revert with AMMStandardHook__PairNotAllowed. The same applies to validateAddLiquidity (AMMStandardHook__LiquidityProviderNotAllowed) and validatePoolCreation (AMMStandardHook__PairNotAllowed or AMMStandardHook__PoolTypeNotAllowed). Any token configured in the registry before the hook was added to the AMM, or any token whose registry.setTokenSettings call did NOT include the hook in hooksToSync, will trigger this permanent DoS on the first hook interaction. The only remedy is an explicit registryUpdateWhitelistPairToken call from the registry to the hook.

coupled_pair.invariant: If hook has pairedTokenWhitelistId=N, hook's _pairTokenWhitelists[N] must contain the same addresses as registry's _pairTokenWhitelists[N]

hypotheses.mechanism: In CreatorHookSettingsRegistry.setTokenSettings (line 376-399), the registry creates a local copy memSettings with initialized forced to true (lines 376-378), then stores memSettings in its own _tokenSettings[token]. However, when syncing to hooks (lines 396-398), it calls IAMMStandardHook(hooksToSync[i]).registryUpdateTokenSettings(token, settings) — passing the ORIGINAL calldata 'settings', NOT 'memSettings'. If the caller supplied settings.initialized=false, the hook receives initialized=false. AMMStandardHook.registryUpdateTokenSettings (line 519-524) writes tokenSettings verbatim without forcing initialized=true. On the next swap, _getOrFetchTokenSettings (line 907-908) sees initialized=false, re-fetches from registry (lines 911-914), and gets the correct HookTokenSettings struct with the new whitelist IDs — but still does NOT populate hook-local whitelist content sets. If the newly pushed settings contain any non-zero pairedTokenWhitelistId pointing to a list whose contents were never pushed to the hook, all direct swaps fail with PairNotAllowed. An authorized token admin can weaponize this by calling setTokenSettings with initialized=false to silently install a permanent DoS via a non-populated whitelist.

coupled_pair.invariant: Hook's initialized flag must always be true after a registry sync, otherwise next swap forces a re-fetch that uses stale empty whitelist contents

hypotheses.mechanism: In AMMStandardHook._validatePricingBounds (line 823-871), the price bounds check reads _pricingBounds[token][pairedToken] from the hook's LOCAL cache (line 829). The opening guard is 'if (bounds.isSet)' (line 830) — if the hook's cache has isSet=false, the ENTIRE bounds check is skipped silently. Pricing bounds are populated in the hook ONLY via registryUpdatePricingBounds (line 546-581), which is triggered by the registry's setPricingBounds (line 523-524) only when hooksToSync includes this specific hook. Critically, the lazy-fetch path _getOrFetchTokenSettings (lines 907-919) NEVER calls any pricing-bounds fetch — it only copies HookTokenSettings. Therefore: if setPricingBounds is called with hooksToSync=[] (or if the hook is added/deployed after bounds are set), the hook has bounds.isSet=false for all pair tokens. All swap-time bounds checks are bypassed entirely. An attacker who observes the on-chain registry state (bounds set in registry) and the hook state (bounds.isSet=false in hook) can execute large swaps at extreme prices that would normally be blocked, causing maximal impermanent loss to LPs who added liquidity expecting price-range protection.

coupled_pair.invariant: If registry has isSet=true bounds for a token pair, hook must also have isSet=true bounds before processing any swaps for that pair

masking_code.masks_invariant: 'if (bounds.isSet)' silently skips the entire price check when local cache is empty, returning no indication that the registry's bounds are being ignored

hypotheses.mechanism: AMMStandardHook.validateHandlerOrder (line 198-226) is invoked by transfer handlers (CLOB, permit) during order creation, NOT by the AMM. It reads _pricingBounds[token][pairedToken] from the hook's LOCAL cache (line 210). There is a notable structural defect: bounds.isSet is checked twice — first at line 211 ('if (bounds.isSet)') and again at line 217 (inner 'if (bounds.isSet)'). The inner check at line 217 can never differ from the outer since no state changes between them; it is unreachable dead code. This fossil suggests the original implementation intended to check a different condition at line 217 — most likely a registry fallback ('else fetch from registry') — but it was never implemented. Without that fallback, any hook with an unsynced _pricingBounds cache has isSet=false, and the entire handler-order price validation is skipped. An attacker who creates a CLOB order at near-zero or near-infinite price against a token with unsynced hook bounds will have their order accepted. When that order fills, the counterparty (pool or LP taking the other side) receives far less than fair value. The attack is parameter-free: no flash loans, no governance, no privileged access required beyond being able to create a CLOB order.

masking_code.masks_invariant: Redundant inner 'if (bounds.isSet)' at line 217 is dead code (identical to outer at line 211) — likely placeholder for a registry-fallback fetch that was never implemented; its absence allows any price when local bounds are unset

hypotheses.mechanism: In CreatorHookSettingsRegistry.updateLpWhitelist (line 689-710) and updatePairTokenWhitelist (line 599-620), the hooksToSync array is fully caller-controlled — provided by the WHITELIST OWNER, not enforced by the registry. When a caller invokes updateLpWhitelist(listId, [bannedLP], false, []) with an empty hooksToSync, the registry's master _lpWhitelists[listId] is updated (bannedLP removed) but NO hooks are notified. AMMStandardHook._enforceLiquidityModificationSettings (line 720-728) reads only the hook's LOCAL _lpWhitelists[lpListId].contains(provider). The banned LP can continue adding liquidity indefinitely through any hook not included in the sync call. Since the hook's _lpWhitelists[id] is ONLY updated via registryUpdateWhitelistLpAddress (callable only by the registry address), and the registry only calls it from updateLpWhitelist/setPricingBounds, a removal is silently ineffective if hooksToSync is empty or incomplete. A sophisticated LP who observes that they have been removed from the registry's master list (e.g., via PairTokenWhitelistUpdated event with add=false) but whose address is still in the hook's local cache (isWhitelistedLiquidityProvider returns true) can continue providing liquidity, collecting fees, and amplifying their position.

coupled_pair.invariant: Removal of an address from registry's _lpWhitelists[id] must propagate to every hook's local cache before any further liquidity operations

hypotheses.mechanism: AMMStandardHook._checkPoolEnabled (line 651-657) makes a LIVE cross-contract call to SETTINGS_REGISTRY.isPoolDisabled(poolId) only when tokenSettings.checkDisabledPools is true. The checkDisabledPools flag is part of the cached HookTokenSettings struct. If the hook's cached struct has checkDisabledPools=false (either because the token was set up that way, or because a settings sync pushed false), then no registry call is ever made regardless of the registry's current disabled state for that pool. CreatorHookSettingsRegistry.setPoolDisabled (line 417-452) updates _disabledPools[poolId] in the registry but has NO mechanism to push this change to hooks or to invalidate hook caches. The only way the hook 'sees' a pool disable is if (a) checkDisabledPools=true in hook cache AND (b) _checkPoolEnabled is called during a swap/liquidity operation. If a token admin calls registry.setPoolDisabled(token, poolId, true) to emergency-halt a pool, but the hook's cached checkDisabledPools=false, the halt is completely ineffective for all hook interactions. Affected participants: token holders expecting the emergency disable to protect them from further adverse trades; LPs who cannot withdraw in time if the pool is being drained.

coupled_pair.invariant: If a pool is disabled in the registry, the hook must enforce that disable regardless of cached checkDisabledPools flag

masking_code.masks_invariant: 'if (tokenSettings.checkDisabledPools)' guard — when cached as false, the live registry disabled-pool check is silently skipped, allowing trading in a pool the registry considers disabled

hypotheses.mechanism: In AMMStandardHook._validatePricingBounds for direct swaps (lines 838-851), when poolType==address(0) (direct swap, no pool), the beforeSwap execution path stores params.amount in transient storage (DIRECT_SWAP_BEFORE_SWAP_AMOUNT_SLOT=0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF) at line 839 and RETURNS EARLY without executing any bounds check. The afterSwap path reads the stored amount and computes the effective execution price from (stored_amount, current_amount) via SqrtPriceCalculator.computeRatioX96 (line 846). If computeRatioX96 overflows it returns 0, and the code reverts (lines 847-850). For non-direct (pool) swaps, the direction-of-travel exemption at lines 858 and 866 allows trades that are moving the price BACK TOWARD valid range even if current price is already outside bounds ('if (zeroForOne || poolType == address(0))' — pool swaps do NOT trigger the strict path when poolType!=address(0)). Direct swaps (poolType==address(0)) always trigger the strict path due to 'poolType == address(0)' in both conditions, so corrective trades via direct swap at out-of-bounds prices are always blocked. Practical impact: if a token's pool price drifts outside bounds, arbitrageurs who want to correct via direct swap will also fail. Only pool swaps (with the direction-of-travel exemption) can be used for price correction, creating a market inefficiency that persists longer than necessary.
